teaser.text: CAE is a company that sells a practical promise: people and machines will be ready when aviation and defence demand them. To see how a dollar comes in and goes out, follow what CAE sells, how it delivers it, and who ultimately pays.

blocks.heading: Where could CAE’s shares be in October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The bear case has a 30% probability. The base case has 50%. The bull case has 20%. By FY2030, management targets C$125–150 million in annual transformation savings and C$950 million–C$1 billion of adjusted segment operating income.

The forecast expects CAE to lose value over one year, recover roughly to today’s price over two, and produce a positive return over three. The weighted price is C$30.75 in October 2027, a 10% loss including dividends. It reaches C$34.49 in October 2028, a 1% gain, then C$40.21 in October 2029, an 18% gain.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for CAE?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives C$650m in 2027 and C$620m in 2028, before recovering to C$650m in 2029. It assumes customer losses, defence delays and late savings. The bull case gives C$800m in 2027, C$880m in 2028 and C$960m in 2029, reflecting higher utilization, funded awards and savings approaching management’s FY2030 target.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for CAE today?

paragraphs.text: On October 18, 2026, C$34.10 at a 26.9x forward P/E implies approximately C$1.27 of next-12-month earnings per share. That is near the upper end of CAE’s FY2027 adjusted EPS guidance of C$1.21–C$1.28. But FY2026 adjusted EPS was C$1.41 under the updated definition, so the forward multiple does not yet prove growth against a consistent base.

blocks.heading: What has CAE guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: FY2027 adjusted EPS guidance is C$1.21–C$1.28. Adjusted segment operating-income margin guidance is 14.6%–15.1%. Management expects cash conversion of 85.0%–95.0%, while Civil revenue is flat to slightly down as training demand softens.

blocks.heading: Has CAE kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The transformation plan now has an early test. CAE targeted C$125 million–C$150 million in annual savings by fiscal 2030, and McLeod reported that six simulators had been retired on the August results call while management retained its targets. These are milestones, not completed savings. CAE also reduced its Civil outlook in November 2025. The fairest judgment is therefore provisional: governance pressure and pay design have improved, but shareholders still need to see promises converted into cash, returns and disciplined decisions.

blocks.heading: What has CAE's revenue and profit trend been?

paragraphs.text: Revenue increased 6.8% to C$1,173.4 million in the June 2026 quarter. Gross margin improved from 28.1% to 29.2%, but operating income fell from C$133.8 million to C$86.8 million.

Civil shows the operational pressure. Revenue rose 5.6%, but adjusted segment operating income fell 13.7%. Its margin declined from 20.2% to 16.5%. CAE cited credit-related charges, a smaller simulator-sales contribution, and weaker joint-venture profitability linked to Middle East disruption.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in CAE's next results?

paragraphs.text: During calendar 2027, investors must also track the expiry or extension of CAE’s NATO flying-training contract and the handoff to FAcT through SkyAlyne. The same trainees may continue receiving instruction, but the entity delivering the work, recording the revenue and receiving the cash may change. That transition, alongside customer retention and cash conversion, will show whether CAE can pay for what comes next.
